title: Do Ukrainian women subject to military service have to leave the EU?
content:
At the end of July, the European Union (EU) did indeed extend temporary protection for people displaced from Ukraine until the 4th of March 2028. At the same time, new applicants for temporary protection will have to be able to demonstrate that they have complied with the military obligations laid down in Ukrainian law.

“Given Ukraine’s evolving defence needs, temporary protection going forward will only be granted to those who have fulfilled their military service obligations in Ukraine,” the Council of the European Union states in its announcement. This can be demonstrated, for example, by a passport containing an exit stamp issued by the Ukrainian authorities showing that the person left Ukraine legally. A paper or electronic document confirming an exemption from military obligations or their fulfilment can also be used as evidence.

title: Is the European Comission planning to confiscate 90% of people’s wealth?
content:
Although Latvia is not among the countries mentioned in the video, one user on the social media platform X has already claimed that “the EC is looking into dekulakisation measures. So that everyone can be equal. Admirable. Let’s tighten our belts and chip in. Some 9 million [euros], not expensive”.

Kužnieks told Delfi that the claims made in the video had been checked by the Representation. The EC is not planning to freeze people’s bank accounts or confiscate 50% or 90% of their wealth, as claimed in the video. The Commission has also not identified any countries where such measures could be introduced first. Nor is the Commission proposing any measures to tax wealth.

The video circulating on social media uses a real study commissioned by the Commission, but its content is interpreted misleadingly. In 2026, the Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union (DG TAXUD) published a study aimed at gaining a better understanding of different wealth-related taxes, their interaction with one another and their effects. It reviews academic literature and analyses the experience of different countries with such taxes.

title: Latvia’s request for a 7 billion euro EU grant remains only an idea for now
content:
Following the publication of the article, many questions arose about whether Latvia had already requested this funding from the EU, when a decision by the EU institutions might be expected and how the money could be spent. However, as Delfi has established, Latvia has not yet discussed the allocation of such funds with EU institutions or other member states – it remains only an idea. Moreover, no meetings specifically devoted to the issue have been planned so far.

According to Politico, Kulbergs’ argument for why the EU should allocate the 7 billion euros to Latvia is that Latvia has to borrow money to ensure the security of countries that are much further from the frontline. The article states that these funds, which Latvia wants in addition to funding already earmarked for other countries, would account for almost half of the planned 15.12 billion euros in defence spending during the new EU multiannual budget period.

However, in comments to Delfi, the prime minister explained that the 7 billion euros is intended in the form of a grant, while stressing that “this is currently only at the level of an idea and discussions between all the eastern-flank countries and the EU are needed”.

title: Sprūds and Ministry of Defence offer different accounts of which “forgotten explosives” were needed for drones
content:
Andris Sprūds is now the Progressives’ lead candidate in the Vidzeme constituency in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Delfi contacted Sprūds and the Ministry of Defence (MoD) to fact-check the claim.

Andris Kulbergs made the claim while answering questions about drone incidents and the work of former Defence Minister Sprūds. Asked whether he was referring to systems purchased during Sprūds’ tenure for which the necessary munitions had not been bought, the prime minister declined to give a specific answer. “We bought the equipment, but forgot to buy the munitions,” Kulbergs said on the programme, adding that such a situation had occurred. He did not name the specific procurement, system, or institution responsible for failing to purchase the ammunition.

The MoD told Delfi that the munitions had not been forgotten. However, a dispute had arisen between the minister and the National Armed Forces (NAF) over their procurement, which had taken up valuable time.

title: “Romania is annexing Moldova”: how frightening disinformation exploded within a few hours
content:
It all began on the 24th of June, when Romania’s lower house of parliament, the Chamber of Deputies, technically deemed a bill submitted by the far-right and pro-Russian party S.O.S. România on the unification of Romania and Moldova to have been “adopted by tacit approval”. The bill stipulates that, once it enters into force, the Romanian government would be authorised to “urgently and immediately” begin negotiations with Chisinau on “completing the union with the Republic of Moldova”, Romanian news portal Digi24 explains.

Before explaining what “tacit approval” means and why such a proposal from a radical party does not have broad political support that would allow it to become law, let us turn to what happened next in the information space.

It took only a few hours for the claim that Romania had effectively begun annexing Moldova to spread like wildfire with the help of various actors and anonymous social media accounts.

title: Czech politician misleads over new EU rules for Ukrainian refugees
content:
Ukrainian men of military conscription age who apply for temporary protection in the EU must now prove that they are fulfilling their military obligations in Ukraine. They also have to be registered in the Reserv+ app. The new requirement applies to applications submitted after 5 August 2026.

The change is part of the EU’s decision to extend temporary protection for Ukrainians fleeing Russia’s war until 2028. It was introduced in response to Ukraine’s military needs.

Jindřich Rajchl, an MP for the ruling SPD party, presented the new rules as a much broader restriction. 

 “Major change in our migration policy! From tomorrow, Ukrainian men of conscription age will no longer be granted temporary protection in the Czech Republic. Personally, I would like to see further changes and tighter rules in this area, and I will fight hard for them. Nevertheless, this is an extremely important step towards ensuring the security of our citizens,” Rajchl wrote in his post.

title: East Flank Podcast #9: Media Freedom on the Eastern Flank
content:
In the latest EastFlank Podcast, journalists from different media outlets across the Eastern Flank discuss media freedom and the challenges facing independent journalism in the region.

How are politics, funding, social media, and changing audience habits reshaping journalism? And are new formats a threat — or an opportunity?

As always, our discussion starts with the latest Collaborative Report, prepared by journalists from across the region. Tune in!

title: Online hate spills into the streets as hate crimes rise in Poland
content:
Not long ago, anti-Ukrainian aggression in Poland was associated mainly with hostile comments online. Recent months, however, have shown that the abuse does not stop there. In July, a 54-year-old man verbally attacked two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls on a city bus in Bielsko-Biała. Prosecutors opened an investigation into the alleged insult of the children on the grounds of their nationality. After reviewing CCTV footage, the city transport operator said the circumstances pointed to a nationality-based motive.

A few weeks later, another case made headlines in Wrocław. On 26 July, a group of men attacked a young Ukrainian couple. Two suspects were detained, and prosecutors brought charges including the use of violence because of the victims’ nationality.

It was not the only such incident in the city. A parliamentary question on violence against Ukrainians listed three incidents in Wrocław between 21 June and 26 July: an air-gun attack on a Ukrainian shop assistant, the beating of a Ukrainian man on Słodowa Island after the attackers heard him speaking Ukrainian, and the previously mentioned brutal assault on the young Ukrainian couple.

title: Poland made billions from the EU carbon market. Where did the money go?
content:
The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is based on a simple principle: if you emit CO₂, you need an allowance to do so. The number of allowances falls each year as the emissions cap is gradually tightened, increasing pressure on companies to invest in low-carbon technologies. The ETS covers the power sector, energy-intensive industries, aviation and, since 2024, shipping – together accounting for around 40 per cent of the EU’s greenhouse gas emissions. Companies can buy, sell and hold allowances.

Since 2013, when the EU carbon market began operating broadly in its current form, member states have collected €270 billion from the system. That is enough money to finance more than one energy transition. The problem is that no one can say exactly where all of it went.

“There is very poor transparency about how this money is being used,” says Greg Van Elsen, senior industrial policy coordinator at CAN Europe. Asked directly whether Europe is making good use of the revenues generated by its own climate policy, his answer is simple: no.

title: Rewriting Slovakia’s history: How pro-Kremlin narratives turn Ukrainians into villains and Russia into saviour
content:
Slovak Agriculture Minister Richard Takáč (Smer-SD) offered a striking reinterpretation of the 1968 Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia during a Sunday debate on TA3. He did so while seeking to deflect criticism of a controversial report on the new Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission.

When opposition MP Alojz Hlina (SaS) pointed out that the report had been announced just days before the anniversary of the Soviet occupation on 21 August, Takáč responded that those who invaded Czechoslovakia “were not troops of the Russian Federation”, but Ukrainian ones.

“What did the Russian Federation have to do with it? The Soviet Union consisted of several countries,” he added then, while also admitting that he was not “exactly a historian”.

No, it was not Ukrainians who came to occupy Czechoslovakia. And although the invading forces came from several Warsaw Pact countries, the decision to intervene was made by the leadership in Moscow. Moreover, the UN Charter still lists the USSR as a permanent member of the UN Security Council. After its dissolution, all sides accepted that Russia would take over its role.

title: Hungarian government has just days left to unlock RRF funds. ‘We will go as far as it takes, and even further if necessary,’ they say
content:
One of the Tisza Party’s most important election promises – and, after taking office, one of its most significant achievements – was to unlock EU funds frozen over corruption under the Viktor Orbán government and concerns about the rule of law.

On May 29, Péter Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reached a political agreement on unlocking €10 billion from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) and €6.4 billion in cohesion funds.

This, however, did not mean that Hungary gained immediate access to the money. Instead, the government committed itself to implementing the reforms and legislative changes required for the funds to be released.

Unlocking the RRF money is the more difficult part, as the deadline for meeting the necessary milestones is August 31, 2026.

Several other EU member states have also struggled with this deadline, but Hungary’s disadvantage had appeared almost impossible to overcome. Negotiations between the Orbán government and the European Commission had progressed extremely slowly, while Budapest had only partially met the requirements, which Brussels deemed insufficient.

title: What consumers need to know about the new rules on repairing household appliances and electronics
content:
The European Union’s new “right to repair” rules, which began to apply in Lithuania at the end of July, aim to create more favourable conditions for repairing faulty products and using them for longer instead of replacing them with new ones.

However, market participants say that the new rules alone may not be enough: as long as repairs remain financially unattractive to consumers and there is a shortage of qualified technicians and convenient infrastructure, repair will not become consumers’ first choice.

Linas Ivanauskas, head of the Electronics Distributors Association (EPA), tells Delfi that the greatest barrier preventing consumers from choosing to repair an item rather than replace it is the fact that repairs are often not financially worthwhile.

title: How Romanians Get Their News: Facebook Leads, TV Wins on Trust
content:
A new analysis by the think tank Expert Forum (EFOR), based on a survey conducted by the Political Rating Agency, paints a more nuanced picture of how Romanians consume information and how social media interacts with traditional news media.

The main finding is that while digital platforms have fundamentally changed how news reaches audiences, they have not replaced traditional sources of information.

Survey data show that television remains the news source Romanians trust the most. Radio and online news outlets also enjoy levels of credibility comparable to – or even higher than – social media platforms.

At the same time, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube have become key gateways through which people discover news. The gap between where people first encounter information and the sources they actually trust reflects one of the defining shifts in today’s media landscape.

title: Civil Defence in Poland: What to Do When Sirens Sound and Drones Are in the Air
content:
The war in Ukraine has made questions that seemed purely theoretical just a few years ago much more real. Repeated incidents involving missiles and drones near or inside Polish airspace show why it is worth knowing what to do when a threat appears over your home.

So what should you do when the sirens suddenly go off? Head to the basement? Get in your car and leave? Wait for an RCB Alert? What if the message never arrives? And who is actually responsible for warning and protecting you?

The answers lie in two rather bureaucratic terms: population protection and civil defence.

Put simply, it is a system designed to make sure that people are not left on their own when a crisis hits.

And it is not just about shelters. Civil defence also means detecting threats, warning the public, organising evacuations and rescue operations, securing water and food supplies, keeping communications running, and making sure emergency services and public authorities are prepared.

There is an important distinction here. As Poland’s government security guide explains, in peacetime Poland operates a population protection system. If martial law is declared or war breaks out, this system becomes civil defence.

title: Hungary’s transformation continues. How Orban’s ousted Baka returned as president?
content:
Since the 9th May, when Peter Magyar’s government replaced Viktor Orban’s 16-year-old administration, Hungary appears to have genuinely entered a new era, with new rules and ambitions. Magyar had promised to do everything possible to bring a “new era” to Hungary, and it is impossible not to notice the sweeping changes. These include the new government’s latest victory: the removal of the Orbán-loyal president from office.

As early as election night in April, Magyar promised to replace the president. At the end of June, alongside plans to draft a new constitution, he announced that he would remove several senior officials from his predecessor Orban’s administration, including Tamas Sulyok.

In an almost hour-long address to parliament in June, the new prime minister announced “Operation Cleansing Fire” to eradicate what he called the “Orban mafia”: “We will rid our country of the economic and political mafia. I consider this my main task.”

title: Latvia’s first public-private partnership project in defence: Lithuania sets an example
content:
Lithuania’s example shows that this is an effective way to promote both the implementation of defence projects and cooperation between the private and public sectors. Latvia is also currently working on implementing its first project of this kind.

Lithuania has accumulated the most experience among the Baltic States in implementing PPP projects in the defence sector, having completed three projects and continuing work on two more. In Latvia, meanwhile, the PPP model in the military sphere is only taking its first steps – the development of part of the infrastructure at the Sēlija military training area could become the country’s first such project.

The use of the PPP regulatory framework in Latvia for implementing various projects of public importance has recently become increasingly active, says Māris Brizgo, associate partner at law firm Ellex Kļaviņš, sworn advocate and head of its public procurement practice group. Although Latvia adopted its PPP law back in 2009, it was not actually used in practice for the first time until 2014, when the Latvian government decided to implement the Ķekava bypass construction project as a PPP.

title: The last shot at Russia came from the grave – who was Lindsey Graham?
content:
In the US press, Lindsey Graham is portrayed as one of the few remaining “old-school” Republicans who managed to maintain an excellent relationship with President Donald Trump without abandoning all of his principles. In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, he is better remembered as a fierce critic of Russia and other authoritarian regimes and, consequently, as a strong friend of the Baltic states, Poland and, above all, Ukraine.

Māris Andžāns, Director of the Centre for Geopolitical Studies, tells Delfi that, in terms of influence, there is now hardly anyone left in US politics who can match Graham as a friend of the region.

Andžāns points out that several factors determine how influential a person is in the US Senate, but one of the most important is how long a senator has served.

title: Different Media Worlds on the Eastern Flank: How Free Is the Press?
content:
Media freedom on the EU’s eastern flank is not one story but many overlapping ones. In some countries, the main worry is concentrated ownership within otherwise open markets. Elsewhere public broadcasters face financial or political pressure, state advertising flows through opaque channels, and politicians increasingly treat journalists as opponents rather than watchdogs.

The sharpest divide is not simply public versus private media. Public broadcasters remain among the most trusted institutions in most Eastern flank countries, while private outlets range from largely independent to vulnerable through ownership, advertising and political rhetoric. The picture shifts visibly from the geographical north toward the south.

title: Czech government scraps EU Information Centres without a clear replacement
content:
A 20-year-old system for communicating about the European Union in the Czech Republic has come to an end. The decision to abolish the Eurocentres was first reported by news site iRozhlas.cz. In mid-August, the plan was presented to the government by Tünde Bartha, head of the Government Office and a close aide to Prime Minister Andrej Babiš (ANO).

“There is no longer a need to have a physical branch and a lot of officials in every region when we are living in a completely different era,” the prime minister said about the abolition of the Eurocentres. They are due to close at the beginning of January next year.
